One consideration that unfortunately no one can add to the other thread:

> Or perform the XSLT transformation on the server side, and serve the resulting HTML to the client. The more long-term solution would be to migrate to a more modern JS/JSON-based framework.

The more "modern" solutions proposed all greatly raise the barrier to entry on the web. The cool thing about XSLT is that it provides a fully static way to add templates to a website (a need everyone immediately comes across once they have more than 2-3 web pages) that you can work your way into piecemeal as you discover your needs without needing build steps or API servers or anything like that. I'm guessing people that program professionally forget that dealing with things like npm, webpack, etc. are way more difficult than wrapping your text in some markup, adding some styles, realizing that you want to extract those out into a stylesheet so you can use them on multiple pages, and eventually coming to understand that you really want to template the whole thing. The old web standards provide a very natural onramp and let you go only as far as you need at any given time. Getting onto the programming language treadmill also pushes security maintenance burden onto authors (who now need to keep on top of regularly updating their frameworks, following the treadmill of paradigm shifts, etc. when they just wanted to make a web site).

The suggestion that someone who wants to make a website should go learn a programming language & frameworks or how to set up a server processing pipeline seems to me to hammer home to idea that individuals are simply no longer relevant to "the web platform". I suppose the writing was on the wall when we gave up on the idea of WYSIWYG editors (remember when Seamonkey had that built right in?) and started normalizing the idea that even simple, completely static web pages like blogs require programming/are not something for the common person to be able to make, but it's still sad.

> Is the low usage statistics of XSLT today an indication of the usefulness of the specification in today's web, or an indication of the challenges of dealing with v1.0 limitations and bugs?

Another factor to consider is whether people are aware of this technology in the first place, and what it is capable of. Personally, when I learned that I can style my RSS feeds to make it user-friendly and include a helpful message at the top explaining what a feed is and how the user can subscribe to it, I immediately applied it to my RSS feed.

As of this issue receiving a lot of attention, I've started informing my fellow developers about XSLT and encouraging them to apply it to their own RSS feeds.

I do agree that something needs to change at least. I set up an XSLT stylesheet for my sitemap last year and it was spectacularly frustrating that there was no clear information anywhere on what features were actually supported by the browsers and the complete lack of feedback when I used an unsupported feature. Sometimes it just hung my entire Firefox process which was unsettling to say the least.
I'm sure at least some of the lack of adoption is caused by developers assuming the entire technology is broken and giving up.

If browser vendors do not have enough resources independently to maintain their XSLT implementations, perhaps resources could be pooled into a single pdf.js style project that could be adopted by all browsers, providing a uniform and consistent experience? Being written in JS would presumably make it easier to provide active feedback to the developer when they make mistakes too. 🙂

I know XSLT has fallen out of favor over the past 20 years, and most developers don’t really care about it anymore. But when it’s used with purpose and skill, it’s incredibly powerful. I’ve been working with XSLT since I first discovered it about ten years ago, and it has become my language of choice for building content-driven websites. I’m sure I’m not entirely alone in this, but sometimes it feels like there are, like, maybe three of us who use XSLT as consistently as I do. And that’s a shame.

XSLT could replace many of the technologies that have been bolted onto the Web platform over the years. With proper browser support for XSLT 3.0 and just a little push in public awareness, it could be a game changer.

There are so many advantages to using XSLT on the Web, but the developer community simply doesn’t know about them. If they did, we might already have full XSLT 3.0 support in browsers. Let’s try to make that happen, then!

One concern I have with an alternative approach leveraging either a polyfill or a browser extension is that either approach lose some of the core features of XSLT.  With XSLT built into browsers, developers have access to a client-side templating engine that is "closer to the metal" _and_ will work when JS is disabled or unavailable in the browser.  Unless I'm mistaken, polyfills and extensions wouldn't work in that scenario and there would be a noticeable performance hit compared to XSLT rendering.

--- 

I'm interested to hear more from engineers with deeper experience in the existing XSLT implementations.

Given the age and general state of the current v1.0 implementations, is it reasonable to assume a v3.0 implementation would be a complete rewrite?

Ignoring resource availability and current priorities, what would a realistic estimate be for the effort it would take to implement and is there an avenue in which one implementation could be used across multiple browsers to spread the effort?

---

One concern with removing XSLT from the web platform entirely is that it means it that not only will the v1.0 implementations be removed, we will likely never see them replaced with the modern specifications.  We do want WHATWG to realistically reflect what browser vendors have implemented or are expecting to implement, if there truly is no interest in supporting XSLT in the future then so be it I suppose.  That is a different conversation compared to security and maintainability of the current implementation, but browser vendors only have so much bandwidth and that's totally reasonable and WHATWG should reflect that if there's vendor consensus.

One area where I think the lack of XSLT support may be more glaring in the future is with the continued growth of LLMs.  If the MCP spec isn't broadly adopted, or if it runs into challenges during adoption, web developers may need a different solution for providing proper REST APIs to LLMs.  XML has gone out of favor, but it is a great fit for that scenario.  I could see a future where we end up developing one semantic REST API providing web page/app state as XML; LLMs interact directly with that gaining what they need from semantic markup and browsers render the exact same state via XSLT stylesheets.  One XML API can serve both use cases, and it does seem like the LLM use case will only grow to a larger piece of the pie in the near future.

cc @mfreed7 

On `disable-output-escaping="yes"`, this is problematic to support because it requires serialization and parsing of the transformed content. For efficiency in a client-side setting, you want a DOM-to-DOM transformation, which is what Gecko does. Possibly, adopting a third-party library that supports XSLT 3.0 would mean switching to a serialize-parse model (and thus theoretically regress performance).

> Are there security concerns relevant to v3.0, or are the concerns limited to the v1.0 specification and current implementations?

I think there's inherent XSS risk with supporting XSLT regardless of version, because the transformed content can execute script and the expectation may be that e.g. RSS is safe.

I think there are also non-security arguments against client-side XSLT, e.g. lack of incremental rendering.

> As a reminder, please read the whatwg [Code of Conduct](https://whatwg.org/code-of-conduct). This issue is intended to be a discussion of alternatives to deprecations and how the concerns raised in [#11523](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11523) may be handled to mitigate the risks for both browser maintainers and users. Please stay on topic here by discussing the pros and cons of XSLT v3.0 support, alternatives, etc. Discussions related to assumed motivations, specific browser vendors, etc. aren't relevant here and will likely just result in the issue being locked, preventing us from having the important discussion in public here.

I don't have a more detailed comment on this issue right now, but I wanted to explicitly say thank you for this portion of your comment, and for the general tone you've created here. It is appreciated.

My reasons for mourning the loss of XSLT:

1.  Many design web component libraries use markup that is modeled after built-in elements, like the table, ul/li, etc.  These web components are beautiful, but the problem is that it's really difficult to make the light DOM children look the same while waiting for the component to download.  With XSLT and just a few lines of very clear instructions, one can let the server be "design library neutral" and ship native table elements, which, with a little styling, can look close to what the design library provides, without the bells and whistles.  Then, when the library has downloaded, apply the XSLT and replace the table with the web components.    Obviously having to download a monstrous polyfill would defeat the purpose.
2. There are scenarios where xslt 3's streaming support would shine, like dynamically building a table of contents as the actual content streams in dynamically.
3. If it could be used in the service worker layer, it could allow bringing in content from third party web sites, and filter out content in an elegant way.  I have another proposal that could do this, but it's just been [sitting there gathering dust](https://github.com/whatwg/dom/issues/1222).  

Why don't the browser vendors do this:  Say how much it would cost to incorporate a library, initially and per year, and see if kickstarter can raise the funds?  I think that would be a much better look, even if sufficient funds aren't raised.

@zcorpan and @mfreed7 thank you both for jumping in here!

> Possibly, adopting a third-party library that supports XSLT 3.0 would mean switching to a serialize-parse model (and thus theoretically regress performance).

Alternatives to in-browser XSLT support would rely on polyfills or browser extensions.  Though adopting third-party libraries would likely mean a performance regression compared to what we have today, would it likely still outperform a polyfill or extension approach?

> I think there's inherent XSS risk with supporting XSLT regardless of version, because the transformed content can execute script and the expectation may be that e.g. RSS is safe.

This concern is particularly interesting to me.  I've viewed the XSS risk similar to that of using `innerHTML` DOM APIs or `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` in react.  Are there situations where XSLT actually poses a more fundamental risk than using `innerHTML` and related wrappers over that API (apologies if I missed examples already given elsewhere in ongoing discussions)?  If so, that seems like a very important example for why deprecating XSLT is more important than updating to the latest specs.

The new Polish e-Invoice will also use the XML format (many government documents do), and with XSLT we can have one community-or-government-made template which everyone could integrate regardless of used technology. It'd also be great if the web browser was able to display just the XML file without any need for additional UI frameworks, it'd reduce the friction to basically zero.

I've learned about XSLT relatively recently, precisely because of this invoice change.. seeing this I was wondering why wasn't it more popular and why so few people were talking about it, but while trying to modify these templates I quickly noticed the limitations of XSLT 1.0 which doesn't even support user functions.
But many don't even know about XSLT at all, especially new developers who might feel overwhelmed by today's complicated web technologies.. the article "XSLT – Native, zero-config build system for the Web" got popular only recently, perhaps because many just didn't know that even existed and was already supported by web browsers?

So I think there's a good opportunity to reduce the barrier to entry for the web by improving XSLT, I genuinely believe this technology has more potential, we just need to give it a proper try!

> I think there's inherent XSS risk with supporting XSLT regardless of version, because the transformed content can execute script and the expectation may be that e.g. RSS is safe.

Oh, it definitely shouldn't be able to execute any JS code..

Regarding implementation details, builtin support via JS/WASM should alleviate security concerns. But for extensions, it should at least be possible to install it with one click instead of being redirected to web store with spammy third-party extensions..

> "closer to the metal" _and_ will work when JS is disabled or unavailable in the browser. Unless I'm mistaken, polyfills and extensions wouldn't work in that scenario and there would be a noticeable performance hit compared to XSLT rendering.

I'm very curious about the impact of polyfills and extensions when the data is XML coming from an embedded device and being transformed by XSLT for a web based control interface or reporting dashboard (which can do things like localisation, text translation for the interface, data visualisations), or to integrate with other systems (like the XML-based APIs used in network devices or medical monitoring systems that get transformed with XSLT into more user friendly formats like HTML or JSON for the systems they integrate with); my understanding is a polyfill isn't going to fit well there and it can't be done serverside when the server is a microcontroller running a web server. Moving to XSLT 3 could unlock a lot more richness for how the data from embedded systems could be used and even a small perf hit from that would presumably be better than the whole data handling having to be reimplented in Java? And like enterprise usage, that also wouldn't show in web stats...

> I'm very curious about the impact of polyfills and extensions when the data is XML coming from an embedded device and being transformed by XSLT for a web based control interface or reporting dashboard

If you can change the `Content-Type` header and serve that as `text/html`, you might be able to use a trick inserting this below the xml-stylesheet directive:
```
<?js-stylesheet /><script src="https://example.com/style.js"></script><!--?><!-- -->
```
and then that `style.js` could generate the page with high flexibility, while the XML file remains valid and can still contain a normal XSLT stylesheet..

But I believe we should go the opposite way - instead of legitimizing the use of JS for such simple cases, we should discourage it by supporting powerful, more user-friendly alternatives such as XSLT 3.0.
JS can do too much and it's difficult for the user to inspect it to ensure only code that serves their interest is allowed to execute, plus it can even interfere with such measures.

> Though adopting third-party libraries would likely mean a performance regression compared to what we have today, would it likely still outperform a polyfill or extension approach?

I think the biggest difference in performance is DOM-to-DOM vs. serialize-transform-parse strategy. The former is better for performance, but the latter is possible to sandbox and therefore likely better for security.

For XSS specifically, it's maybe about the same as `innerHTML`, however there are other classes of security bugs reported for XSLT that don't apply to `innerHTML`, e.g.: reading local files, various UAF bugs, bypassing CSP, etc.

Since XSLT 3.0 has more features than 1.0, in theory it means more attack surface. Some classes of bugs could be addressed by using an implementation written in a memory-safe language + sandboxing, though.

The phenomenon of XSLT implementations getting stuck at XSLT 1.0 is broader than just browsers:

Xalan is at XSLT 1.0. According to Wikipedia, "Microsoft provides two XSLT processors (both XSLT 1.0 only)."

Adding XSLT 3.0 support either in the context of libxslt (WebKit and Chromium) or Transformiix (Gecko) doesn't make sense from the point of view of the current technical state of libxslt or Transformiix or as a matter of the amount of effort needed vs. the benefit and considering the opportunity cost of what else could be accomplished in Web browser development with that amount of effort.

Which makes the question

> Are there external libraries that browsers could adopt in order to gain v3.0 support without building and maintaining the specification in house?

relevant.

Setting aside for the moment the question of whether the benefit would be worth the integration effort, let's look at the other requirements:

First there's the question of level of integration vs. performance. Gecko currently has much deeper integration of the XSLT engine with the browser internals: The XSLT engine operates on the browser DOM implementation. WebKit and Chromium integrate with libxslt in a way that's inherently bad for performance: The XSLT engine doesn't operate on the browser DOM but the XSLT engine and the rest of the browser communicate via XML as serialized as text. The Gecko approach gives rise to opportunities for security bugs (due to both XSLT and JS having access to the same DOM) that the inherently-bad-for-performance XSLT integration architecture that WebKit and Chromium use protects from.

So perhaps worse is better and we don't even need to constrain the search for an external library to one that could operate on an externally-provided XML tree (i.e. the browser DOM)!

But there are still real constraints left (list possibly not exhaustive!):

1. The external library needs to be under an Open Source license (and likely one that doesn't have provisions that would make the exact manner of integration a license matter in addition to being a technical matter) and the preferred form for making modifications needs to actually be available.
2. The external library needs to implement enough XSLT 1.0 and EXSLT compatibility that existing Web content written for libxslt and Tranformiix keeps working.
3. The external library needs to use a programming language that fits the memory-safety requirements and engineering practices of Web browsers. (That is, even implementation in a safe language isn't OK if browsers don't otherwise contain code in that particular safe language and adding the capability to use code in that language would be involve high up front and ongoing cost.)

I'm not aware of any existing XSLT 3.0 implementation that satisfies those three rather basic constraints.

(Typically Xee is suggested as the solution. At this time, it fails the second constraint. I can't speak for Safari, but it might also fail the third constraint for Safari.)

> The phenomenon of XSLT
implementations getting stuck at XSLT 1.0 is broader than just browsers:

To expand on this a bit if you look at any runtime with XSLT built-in: e.g. Java, PHP, .net they're all limited to XSLT 1.0 (happy to be corrected)

PHP for example is using libxslt the same library as chromium and WebKit.

Other third-party libraries that are used for other languages like python's lxml also don't support more than libxslt 1.0 (they're also based on libxslt).

If there was an obvious convergence on a specific V2 or V3 implementation then it might make more sense but if nothing else has made the move to integrate a newer version it probably presents more work for browsers if they were to be the first (and possibly only) to do that.

I've tagged this as https://github.com/whatwg/html/labels/addition%2Fproposal because this is a request to adopt XSLT 3.0, but also I've tagged it https://github.com/whatwg/html/labels/needs%20implementer%20interest to clarify the fact that right no there are no browser implementers who have agreed to take a supportive position of implementing XSLT 3.0. This is a procedural matter, for the purposes of issue triage in the WHATWG HTML issue tracker.

Usually for feature requests we'd ask that you follow the template provided, and as a policy matter tend to close issues out, asking them to be re-opened with the template, but I am conscious that might be seen as me attempting to silence discourse, so I'm going to avoid doing so in this instance. However, to anyone reading this, if you're interested in raising new feature requests for the standard please use the [new feature issue template](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/new?template=1-new-feature.yml).

I strongly support the proposal. 

The community using XSLT is vibrant and growing. The difference between version 2.0 and 1.0 is night and day. Version 3.0, with first class support for arrays and maps, provides highly performative transformations in a declarative mode. Version 4.0 is under development right now: https://qt4cg.org/

XSLT 1.0 is extremely limited, and difficult to work with. More recent versions are delightfully expressive and powerful, and open up to ordinary people the ability to do highly complex styling and transformation. With XSLT 3.0 it is possible to do things that are very, very challenging to do in Javascript and other browser-supported technologies.

I appreciated learning about the security flaws pointed out by Frantric in his talk, but I disagree on the diagnosis. In my opinion, the problem is not with XSLT, but with old technology, and the underlying rules that dictate how XSLT and Javascript are allowed to interact.

I also strongly support the idea of creating a new implementation of XSLT 3.0 in a memory-safe language and integrating it into browsers as part of the standard. I don't see how security is more of an issue with XSLT than it would be with JS, which can similarly rewrite the entire DOM of a web page and introduce any content it likes. In addition to the RSS-feed community, there are text-encoders, document curators, and digital edition specialists all over the world generating large quantities of HTML content statically offline using e.g. the Saxon XSLT processor, then pushing it to web servers; the benefits of being able to do this work in the client browser would be huge. The ability to offer different versions or configurations of entire sites based on user needs and preferences, but based on a single XML source, would be very powerful.

There are several additional points.

1. Lack of implementer interest is sad, but it's nothing that cannot be fixed. SVG was in limbo for *a long time* (IIRC there was talk of removing it from the spec, too), but then interest picked up, and now SVGs are an indispensable part of the web
2. There's currently literally a discussion on implementing a new templating system for the web. See https://justinfagnani.com/2025/06/30/what-should-a-dom-templating-api-look-like/ and https://github.com/WICG/webcomponents/issues/1069 when we already have a powerful templating system that can be native to the browser and even work without JS if needed.

I'm someone who regularly teaches XPath and XSLT 3.0 (and looking ahead to 4.0) in the context of a Digital Media program that combines Digital Arts and Digital Humanities. In my world, the teaching of XSLT is part of Digital Humanities coursework and associated with document data modeling, digital publishing, and media transformations. It looks like this is where you're observing the most evidence of the ongoing relevance of client XSLT in the browser, with RSS feeds and podcasts, but as @martindholmes mentions, there are other uses in developing static websites and also in transformations to scalable vector graphics (SVG). In my university program, XSLT is very much about style and design templating, a language that our students learn to design with as a creative medium alongside CSS.

We haven't been trying the old XSLT 1.0 browser clients, but that's because they're outdated. Instead we tend to run XSLT transformations before publishing to the web. If we had a viable 3.0 client that would be amazing. As @Arithmeticus observes, XSLT 3.0 is especially powerful for outputting maps and arrays (and 4.0 will be even more convenient): It's efficient and practical for those who need intricate JSON structures, for designing JavaScript-based web interfaces as well as in making knowledge graphs and feeding "ground truth" data to LLMs. 

So in my program I'm finding XSLT increasingly important to teach for that reason: Stylesheet templating in XSLT 3.0 is a powerful way to learn how to express a JSON map structure working with markup source data. This fall, we'll be teaching XSLT 3.0 right alongside Node JS applications, and these are both complementary power-tools for our students. The latest XSLT is also taught at XML Summer School and other venues attracting Digital Humanities people like me. The current XSLT is a highly preferred and accessible programming idiom for those "in the know" about it.

So very much this. It's easy to let something wither and die on the vine, and then complain "we should get rid of this dead branch" while ignoring that it died from neglect. Given the extent to which browsers neglected to include support for newer version of XSLT and/or actively hid / downplayed the ability to use XSLT in the browser, I think this is a fair analogy. 

OTOH, I'd almost rather see the web platform revisit extension mechanisms and focus on finding a safe and efficient way for browser users to extend their browsers with new / unique capabilities without needing to be dependent on the browser manufacturers. Let me plug in support for XSLT, or MNG, or *gasp* Java, or whatever if I want, and this becomes much less of an issue.

@mindcrime The problem with making such functionality an optional user-controlled component is that no-one can then build a website that depends on it, because most of their users won't have it. Imagine if JavaScript support were provided by optional plugins that didn't ship with browsers. Most of the web would simply not work. If we want XSLT support to be robust, it has to be part of the standard, IMHO.

I also agree that this extension should be bundled (I don't think they'd be happy if you needed to install a third party extension to view Google Ads :)

But note that with unbundled extensions, there's still a difference between:
a) having a simple dialog like "this page needs extension X to run, do you want to install it?" (just like with encrypted media on linux)
b) a dialog redirecting to a particular extension created by a browser vendor
c) a dialog redirecting to "web store" where you find various spammy extensions that will be sold in the future
d) no dialog at all, forcing the user to search the web, finding SEO spam / AI slop

So if they don't want to bundle it, let's at least try to persuade them into implementing a) or in the worst case b).

>The phenomenon of XSLT implementations getting stuck at XSLT 1.0 is broader than just browsers

Indeed, there were at least a dozen serious implementations of XSLT 1.0, and very few of them advanced much beyond that level. The reasons were not technical but economic: the corporate implementations (from Microsoft, Oracle, IBM et al) were either free, making it hard to construct a business case for ongoing development, or (like IBM Datapower and Websphere) very expensive, leaving them with a niche market and little visibility. The hobbyist implementations (of which libxslt was one) never found a source of income to fund ongoing development. The fact that my company, Saxonica, is almost alone in moving the technology forward today is largely due to the fact that we found a successful business model that converted user added-value into development investment. I have to confess I have never understood the economic drivers for the web browser vendors, but it's always economics that drives technology forward.

There are many, many serious users of XSLT, both in the domain of specialist publishing where its benefits are well understood by that user community, and in financial applications such as XBRL and e-invoicing where XML-based data interchange standards are deeply embedded. Casual use for applications with less complex requirements has probably dropped off, though of course we can only guess at actual numbers. The serious users, of course, are the ones who gain benefit from the enhanced functionality of the 2.0 and 3.0 standards, and who drive the requirements for 4.0 which is under development. But the vast majority of serious users do their XML processing on the server, either "on demand" in the web server, or further upstream in the publishing workflow. Probably the biggest reason for this is the poor level of support for XSLT in the browser: it's not surprising to see low levels of usage when the technology on offer has been stagnant for 20 years. How many people would be using Javascript if it had been left untouched for so long?

There is another factor here which needs to be mentioned: although XSLT has advanced greatly since 1.0, the language standard has not evolved to provide the kind of capabilities needed for modern interactive web applications. It is still very much a document-to-document transformation language. With our SaxonJS product we have demonstrated that client-side XSLT can go beyond this, (a) by supporting event-driven user-interface interactivity, and (b) by providing asynchronous resource access for data integration: both features essential to modern web applications. But such features haven't found their way into the standards, and this is because we're pretty well the only people driving the technology forward in this space. And we haven't been driving it as hard as I would like, because unlike our server-based products, we have found it very hard to find a revenue stream to feed the investment.

I believe that the security concerns regarding XSLT in the browser are entirely specific to the particular implementations such as libxslt. There is no intrinsic reason why XSLT should be less secure than Javascript; on the contrary, as a purely declarative language it should be intrinsically easier to sandbox.

The exslt support needed for browser compatibility is very minimal. And for example xee is likely to be close to having enough XSLT 1 support soon, and with encouragement no doubt it could happen sooner.

There are three compatibility cases in practice:

1. XSLT 1 fed to an XSLT 1 processor, which is the status quo;
2. XSLT 1 fed to an XSLT 3 processor and marked as XSLT 1, so the XSLT 3 processor can run in compatibility mode (as defined by the XSLT spec), or can delegate to an XSLT 1 implementation;
3. XSLT 1 fed to an XSLT 3 processor but nor marked as XSLT 1 - e.g. with `version=3` in it. In this case it will still work correctly in almost all cases - the most significant differences are around whitespace handling informed by DTD validation, which browsers don’t perform anyway. Backwards compatibility was considered very carefully.

A test suite would be helpful here.

There’s also questions around JavaScript functions made visible to XPath inside XSLT, but i think that may have been IE-only. None the less, it's useful and adds a greater degree of integration with the Web platform.

XML and XSLT are tools that, when used as we intended them to be used :-) enable people who don’t think of themselves as programmers to do advanced text processing and to make relatively sophisticated applications. So i don’t see XSLT as a failed competitor to JavaScript. I see it as a target market of people who are currently under-served, and a way to draw people and communities closer.

>The exslt support needed for browser compatibility is very minimal

A more problematic issue is the poorly-thought-out WHATWG "willful violation" of the XPath 1.0 specification regarding namespaces.

I would like to echo the comment about XSLT in the Digital Humanities. We've built an entire catalogue of Indian manuscripts (mostly Sanskrit and Tamil) in TEI XML, rendered client-side in the browser using XSLT 1.0:

https://tst-project.github.io/collections/bnf/

These manuscript descriptions were then uploaded to the site of the National Library of France, converted using XSLT 1.0:

https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc112191c

While I would very much welcome browser support of XSLT 3.0, I would also like to point out how powerful XSLT 1.0 in the browser already is, as the above examples show. While there are a number of things to be aware of, such as browser-specific implementation details, this article was immensely useful:

https://www.balisage.net/Proceedings/vol21/print/Thompson01/BalisageVol21-Thompson01.html

Many projects in the humanities sector rely on x-technology stacks. In my relatively small nieche (digital edition projects, mostly related to cultural heritage) it affects at least 1,000 projects. As XSLT 1.0 had some limits, many projects migrated to XSLT 2.0 or 3.0 using server-side transformation, which causes a lot of maintenance costs. There are also some JavaScript based solutions, but they perform weak in larger projects. It would be a lot more sustainable with native XSLT support in the browser.

I'm also strongly in favor of adopting XSLT 3.0.

Ideally, this should also

* include support for newer revisions of the standard as they get released (for example, [4.0](https://qt4cg.org/specifications/xslt-40/Overview.html#whats-new-in-xslt4) which, as mentioned, is already in the works);

* cover also XSLT application to HTML (i.e. regardless if the DOM is assembled from an HTML5 or XHTML serialization),
which may be introduced via the usual processing instructions (either in XML or SGML form).

One benefit of adopting XSLT 3.0 that I haven't seen mentioned here is that, if the implementation supports XPath 3.1, the language can also be used [to process JSON data](https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-30/#json) directly.

Concerning @zcorpan's security concerns:

> For XSS specifically, it's maybe about the same as `innerHTML`, however there are other classes of security bugs reported for XSLT that don't apply to `innerHTML`, e.g.: reading local files, various UAF bugs, bypassing CSP, etc.

> Since XSLT 3.0 has more features than 1.0, in theory it means more attack surface. Some classes of bugs could be addressed by using an implementation written in a memory-safe language + sandboxing, though.

Indeed, and this is also another advantage of the DOM-to-DOM approach (in addition to performance and the applicability of XSLT to “plain” HTML): it can be run with similar sandboxing conditions as JavaScript (potentially even the same sandbox, depending on how XSLT support and JS are implemented), making it no less secure than JS in that regard.

Concerning @hsivonen point about existing libraries:

The Semantic Web promised a universal layer of machine-readable meaning. Still, that effort largely failed due to its complexity and the lack of foundational upper ontologies to draw on. 

At the same time, diverse communities have quietly built large sets of documents in domain-specific XML vocabularies such as TEI, JATS, and countless others that encode semantics in a structured but approachable way.
LLMs and other AI systems thrive on clean, structured, and semantically annotated data. Yet the web is awash in HTML optimized for presentation rather than meaning. 

With the `xml-stylesheet` processing instructions (PIs), semantically rich XML can be associated directly with its transformations into HTML, delivering a user-friendly view while preserving the machine-readable source on the web.

 This model provides a dual value stream:
- **Humans** receive (re)structured, styled, usable content in HTML.
- **Machines** (scrapers, AIs, and other processors) can read the original XML containing domain-specific metadata according to its schema (DTD/XSD/RNG).
 
Aside: It is true that JSON is also machine-readable, but its access is mediated through JavaScript. Extracting data from a JSON-fed web application typically requires reverse-engineering API calls, reconstructing state, and navigating the application’s logic (e.g., through headless browsers).

XML + XSLT provides many advantages, to name a few:
* **Directness**: the XML document *is* the data.
* **Declarativity**: The XSLT is a purely declarative transformation; XML is married to its derivative.
* **Stability**: Scrapers and downstream processors can target the XML directly, without dependency on the application code, which is subject to change.

This makes the XML + XSLT model more transparent and more hospitable to automated processing by search engines, research tools, and AI agents.

## Why hasn't this happened already?

It is true that browsers already shipped with XSLT 1.0 two decades ago. However this approach never realized its potential, not because the idea was flawed, but because the implementation froze at the relatively limited 1999 standard. 

XSLT 3.0 resolves many of these. I will detail them in a separate post, but the TL;DR:
* XPath 1.0 was much more limited, and more code had to be pushed into the XSLT layer, which is bad because…
* XSLT 1.0 is much more verbose than XSLT 2.0+

In other words, the browser implementations never evolved alongside the XML ecosystem. Communities that might have built workflows around XML + XSLT in the browser simply went elsewhere.

Standardizing browser support for XSLT 3.0 would realign the web with its original dual mandate: to serve both people and machines. It would incentivize communities to publish semantically rich XML, ensuring that the ground truth of their data remains accessible not only for presentation, but for reasoning, search, and machine learning.

**The web ultimately produces what its architecture rewards.**

If the platform adopts XSLT 3.0, the effort should incorporate lesson(s) learned from `XSLTProcessor`, IMO -- the new API should feature a) _granularity_ and b) _transparency_. Both are related, admittedly, but let me elaborate. This is orthogonal to the XSLT version support.

The `importStylesheet` method of `XSLTProcessor`, for instance, is a hammer -- once your [XSL] stylesheet is imported, available processing is largely a "black box" -- there is no way to invoke a specific template imported as part of the stylesheet, on an arbitrary node set, for example. It's a classic problem of "assuming application" -- XSLT can and should be used to support _applications_, but it's hard to predict the scope and kind of these, which is why the design of an XSLT API that may or may not implement a sufficiently capable revision of XSLT, is so important. I don't intend to teach and preach, but this is in part what [Hyrum's Law](https://www.hyrumslaw.com/) is about. Using `XSLTProcessor` for anything else but transforming _entire documents_ with XSLT 1.0, is an exercise in frustration. One may ask -- well, isn't transforming documents _exactly_ what XSLT is about -- no more and no less? Yes, but what if I want to leverage XSLT as part of e.g. a template processing engine that is expressed in the form of HTML (5) custom element(s) -- I will need to go through hoops applying `XSLTProcessor` specifically, in elaborate ways, in order to accomplish anything useful. I know this because I've tried this.

The new API would benefit from containing multiple, inter-operating classes that offer processing granularity to facilitate broad range of applications while still being contained in its scope to, well, XSLT. I am sure there's a practical limit for how much granularity can be put into the API (abstract) before the design starts to impair performance allowed to implementation(s), but there's no way to tell before a concrete proposal is up for review. All I know is that API "granularity" and performance sometimes end up at the crossroads.

Transparency, being related to granularity, would help troubleshooting, as you'd be dealing with constructs of "finer" size and would thus be able to assume more context for when things go wrong -- applying a single template of your choosing, for example, would tell you that the error necessarily comes from applying that template and not the potentially much larger stylesheet, likely related to the node set you're passing or the parameters of invocation [of the template].

With the above in mind, this brings me to the second point:

I believe the better practical alternative is to actually then **keep XSLT out of the Web browser**, although I am not sure what to do with `XSLTProcessor` that is there today. Instead (re-)introduce some hooking for those of us who, as has been voiced elsewhere, prefer to use XSLT _without_ explicit client-side scripting but for simply rendering an XML document served by the browser. I mean, I do believe it's a legitimate application that is still relevant, but if possible, should be left to a third-party.

The Web platform has an obesity crisis, and in generally I think we should be _removing_ APIs, not adding them, not where loading third-party code can be a substitute. On a related note, effort should be put in facilitating development of third-party libraries even for areas where performance is critical. WebAssembly has been a step in the right direction there, and people working on it have realized the importance of inter-operability with the [JavaScript] host, and are developing further there. The latter aspect, for example, is more important for e.g. XSLT which operates on DOM nodes and not fundamental data atoms like characters or bytes, which WASM otherwise is capable of processing at least as fast as JavaScript. So for XSLT, a well-developed platform for facilitating development of "fast" third-party library code, is paramount. An XSLT 3.0 processor that is "too slow", won't do it any favours. Then the argument will necessarily shift back to the original "should the Web platform adopt XSLT 3.0", which IMO is bit of acknowledging defeat.

So for XSLT, for example, one may ask if a sufficiently performant XSLT 3.0 processor can be written with WebAssembly? Or even JavaScript? I guess there's only one way to find out.

Again, to reiterate, I assume that a third-party XSLT processor can be plugged into the browser in a manner that allows it to transform even top-level loaded (navigation) XML documents that feature an XSL stylesheet link. It might require scripting support, admittedly -- you can't have third-party code without client-side scripting host _and/or_ WASM machine. Unless you resort to plugins, but I think that door has been closed for good, at least in the case with the modern Web browser.

Leaving XSLT to third-parties obviously absolves the platform of responsibility over both the API standard, maintaining the code, and leaves people to implement (and optimize) XSLT, including possibly adding features that would be specific to XSLT "on the Web". Like for example JavaScript functions for extension, that are able to use node sets (as parameters and return value both).

Please take the good with the bad here -- I am merely offering my personal perspective, for your deliberation. My background is that I've been using XSLT on and off since 2002, with XML and then HTML on the Web first then playing with `libxslt`, and recently trying it with HTML 5 (with mixed success) using both server- and client- side processing.

It is motivated by the desire to have implementations be compatible with legacy HTML content while still supporting the changes that this specification introduces to HTML regarding the namespace used for HTML elements, and by the desire to use XPath 1.0 rather than XPath 2.0.

So i don’t see a problem in explicitly allowing an implementation to do this, nor in configuring a default for XPath 2 or later in browsers. Any API in a browser allowing XPath 2 3 or 4 would need a mechanism for saying which XPath version is to be used, and perhaps for passing in a map of default options.

The problems with the statement "If the context node is from an HTML DOM, the default element namespace is `http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml`. are that (a) you need to extend the data model to recognize there are two kinds of nodes, XML nodes and HTML nodes, and (b) you need to change the default element namespace to be a dynamic concept rather than a static one (because it depends on runtime data). But more fundamentally, you need to explain what "the context node" means here: is it the context node for an XPath expression as a whole, or the context node for an individual axis step? Either way, it gets very confusing when you do joins across multiple documents (something, of course, that XPath 1.0 can't really handle).

The assertion that "This is equivalent to adding the default element namespace feature of XPath 2.0 to XPath 1.0" is just plain ignorant.

Since a mapping is needed from the HTML DOM to XDM anyway, the whole thing could have been handled much more easily (and conformantly) by mapping HTML elements to no-namespace XDM elements.
